slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)  ·  Units: mg/dL

What it is used for: CRP shows how much inflammation is present in the body. It is ordered with symptoms of a bacterial infection (fever or chills, rapid heart rate, rapid breathing, nausea and vomiting), to check for a chronic inflammatory condition, to monitor for infection after surgery, to follow a condition and its treatment, and to help make treatment decisions in sepsis.
CRP rises and falls with the amount of inflammation, so a falling CRP suggests that treatment is working or that the body is healing on its own.

slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: CRP is made by the liver in response to inflammation. Short-lived acute inflammation helps tissues heal from injury or infection, whereas long-lasting (chronic) inflammation can damage healthy tissue; it is most often caused by autoimmune disorders, but also by repeated injury or irritation, for example from smoking.

slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: High CRP may indicate an acute or chronic condition, such as bacterial or viral infections, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis), autoimmune disorders (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis) or lung diseases such as asthma. Smoking and exposure to environmental toxins, such as polluted air, can also raise CRP.

High: Healthy people usually have very low CRP, and any increase may mean inflammation. Increases have also been linked to insomnia, depression, hormone therapy for menopause and obesity, and females often have slightly higher CRP than males.

slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Interferences: Some medicines and supplements may affect the result; tell the provider about everything taken, including magnesium and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and aspirin. Prescription medicines should not be stopped without talking with the provider.
Limitations: CRP shows how much inflammation there is, but not its cause or location. A diagnosis requires other test results, symptoms and medical history.
A standard CRP test should not be confused with a high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) test. Both measure CRP, but hs-CRP detects very small increases and is used to estimate the risk of heart disease.

slides.title: Rheumatoid factor (RF)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: The RF test is mostly used with other tests to help diagnose rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a chronic autoimmune disorder that damages joints and causes pain, swelling and stiffness and can also affect organs. It can also be used to check for other autoimmune disorders, certain infections and certain cancers.

slides.title: Rheumatoid factor (RF)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: It is ordered with symptoms of RA: joint pain or stiffness when moving (worse in the morning or after inactivity, usually on both sides), tender, red and warm joints, swelling that makes daily tasks hard, fatigue, fever, loss of appetite, and hard bumps under the skin near joints. Because RA often causes anemia, it may be ordered for anemia too. It is rare to test RF without symptoms.

slides.title: Rheumatoid factor (RF)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Physiology: Rheumatoid factor is a protein made by the immune system. Ordinary antibodies attack germs, but RF attacks healthy cells — usually IgG, one of the most common antibodies. The immune system makes it by mistake or when it is overactive fighting an infection. Many healthy people have small amounts of RF, and even high amounts are not always a sign of disease.

slides.title: Rheumatoid factor (RF)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · Interpreting the result
bullets: Positive result: A positive result means a higher level of RF was found. Using other tests, symptoms and history, the provider looks for RA or another autoimmune disease (Sjögren syndrome, lupus, scleroderma, juvenile idiopathic arthritis in children), a chronic infection (hepatitis C, tuberculosis, endocarditis) or certain cancers (such as leukemia). Generally, the higher the RF, the more likely a condition linked to it.
Negative result: A negative (normal) result means little or no RF, but it does not rule out RA or another problem. With RA symptoms and a normal RF, the provider may order more tests.

slides.title: Rheumatoid factor (RF)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed; blood is drawn from a vein. At-home kits (finger-prick blood mailed to a lab) are also available — share the result with your provider.

Limitations: An RF result alone cannot diagnose a condition. People with RA can have little or no RF, and people without RA can have a lot. If the result is reported as an amount, the report may give that laboratory’s normal range. With inconclusive results the provider may refer you to a rheumatologist.

slides.title: Rheumatoid factor (RF)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: RF is found in other autoimmune diseases and even in some healthy people, while some people with RA have little to none. So the anti-CCP test is done with or after RF: together the two tests give a more accurate diagnosis than RF alone.
The RF test is not used to diagnose osteoarthritis, which is not an autoimmune disease and does not involve rheumatoid factor.

slides.title: Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Blood serum

What it is used for: According to the WHO expert report, streptococcal antibody tests (ASO, anti-DNase B) are not needed for uncomplicated streptococcal upper respiratory infection; they are used to document a preceding streptococcal infection in suspected acute rheumatic fever and should be done in every such patient. The most commonly performed, commercially available tests are ASO and anti-DNase B.

slides.title: Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Per CDC, diagnosing acute rheumatic fever (together with the Jones criteria) usually needs evidence of a preceding group A strep infection: a positive throat culture or rapid antigen test, or an elevated or rising streptococcal antibody titer. In post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, elevated streptococcal antibodies are also one form of evidence of the preceding infection.

Physiology: ASO is an antibody to streptolysin O, an extracellular antigen of group A streptococci. Titres of ASO, anti-DNase B and other antibodies to streptococcal extracellular antigens peak 3–4 weeks after the acute infection and usually stay up for 2–3 months before declining.

slides.title: Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Acute rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis are delayed, immune-mediated sequelae of group A strep pharyngitis or skin infection. Rheumatic fever usually follows the infection by 1–5 weeks; glomerulonephritis follows pharyngitis by about 10 days and skin infection by up to 3 weeks.

slides.title: Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: At least one anti-streptococcal antibody titre should be elevated for a diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever. A titre is elevated if it exceeds the upper limit of normal for the community (the titre exceeded by no more than 20% of the population). When two antibody tests are used, both are elevated in most cases.

slides.title: Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Limitations: A single elevated titre may document a previous streptococcal infection, but a further test 3–4 weeks after the onset of rheumatic fever is recommended. About 20% of people with a first attack and most patients with chorea alone have low ASO titres — which is why a second antibody test (anti-DNase B) helps.

The normal range varies with age, geographic locale and season; the upper limit is set by measuring titres in sera from people of the right age group without a recent streptococcal infection. A reference serum with a known titre is run as a control with each set. So there is no universal number — use the laboratory reference on the result report.

slides.title: Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Antibodies such as ASO can only be interpreted in retrospect, so they are of little or no use for diagnosing acute strep pharyngitis or tonsillitis. Per CDC there is no definitive diagnostic test for acute rheumatic fever: the diagnosis is clinical, using the 2015 revised Jones criteria — an elevated ASO alone is not a diagnosis.

slides.title: Cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody (anti-CCP)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: The anti-CCP test helps diagnose or rule out rheumatoid arthritis. It is often done with or after an RF test, and when other tests could not confirm or rule out RA. Symptoms include joint pain, stiffness (especially in the morning), joint swelling, fatigue and low-grade fever.

Physiology: CCP antibodies (anti-CCP) are autoantibodies — abnormal proteins that attack healthy cells by mistake instead of protecting the body. They target healthy joint tissue. Anti-CCP is found in most people with rheumatoid arthritis and almost never in people who do not have it.

slides.title: Cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody (anti-CCP)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · Interpreting the result
bullets: Positive result: In someone with RA symptoms: anti-CCP positive and RF positive — probably RA; anti-CCP positive and RF negative — possibly early RA or RA that will develop in the future. The result is read together with the RF result and a physical exam.
Negative result: With anti-CCP negative and RF negative, RA is less likely; the provider may order more tests to find the cause of the symptoms.

slides.title: Cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody (anti-CCP)
slides.eyebrow: Autoimmune and rheumatology · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines, vitamins and dietary supplements: you may need to stop certain substances for 8 hours before the test.

Limitations: Anti-CCP may also be found in other conditions: other autoimmune disorders (Sjögren syndrome, lupus), active tuberculosis and chronic lung disease. To understand the result, the provider considers symptoms, history, physical exam and other tests.
RA can be hard to diagnose, especially early. Besides anti-CCP and RF, the provider may order joint x-rays and tests such as ESR, synovial fluid analysis, C-reactive protein and antinuclear antibody.

slides.title: Rheumatoid arthritis
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Overview
bullets: With rheumatoid arthritis symptoms, lab results are judged with symptoms and a physical exam: RF and anti-CCP are interpreted together.

slides.title: Rheumatoid arthritis

Used to help diagnose or rule out rheumatoid arthritis; often done with or after an RF test.
Shows how much inflammation there is; high CRP occurs in autoimmune disorders (lupus, RA, vasculitis).

slides.title: Rheumatoid arthritis

slides.eyebrow: Condition · Cautions
bullets: A negative RF does not rule out rheumatoid arthritis: people with RA can have little or no RF.

slides.title: A patient's CRP is high. What does this result tell you on its own?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: It confirms a bacterial infection, although it cannot show where it is located
It shows that inflammation is present, but not its cause or location
It identifies which organ is inflamed and what is causing it
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: for a diagnosis, CRP is interpreted with other tests, symptoms and medical history.

Basis: MedlinePlus: CRP results show how much inflammation there is, but not what is causing it or where it is.

slides.title: How does a standard CRP test differ from a high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) test?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Both measure CRP, but hs-CRP detects very small increases and is used to estimate heart disease risk
hs-CRP measures a different protein, made by the heart, that signals heart disease risk
hs-CRP is the test used for treatment decisions in sepsis, because it detects smaller changes than CRP
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the tests measure the same protein but are used for different conditions.

Basis: MedlinePlus: CRP and hs-CRP tests both measure CRP but are used for different conditions; hs-CRP measures very tiny increases and estimates heart disease risk.

slides.title: RA symptoms, anti-CCP positive, RF negative. What may this mean per MedlinePlus?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Early RA or RA that will develop later
Rheumatoid arthritis is fully ruled out because RF is negative, so no other tests are needed
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. That is the source’s reading; the final assessment uses the exam and other tests.

Basis: Anti-CCP is almost never found without RA; some people with RA have no RF.

slides.title: Why is ASO of little use for diagnosing acute strep pharyngitis?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: ASO is measured only in urine
ASO is high in all healthy people, so it cannot be interpreted for any purpose
The titre rises late and can only be read in retrospect
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. That is why ASO is used to document a preceding infection in rheumatic fever, not in acute pharyngitis.

Basis: Antibody titres peak 3–4 weeks after infection and are read in retrospect.

slides.title: C-reactive protein:
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: is present normally, decreases in inflammation
appears in tissue necrosis and inflammatory processes
decreases during remission of the inflammatory process
decreases at the height of the disease

slides.title: Determining CRP, RF, ASO. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. CRP is an acute-phase protein; immunoturbidimetry/nephelometry (quantitative) or latex agglutination (semi-quantitative); <3 mg/L normal; rises sharply in bacterial infection; hs-CRP – cardiovascular risk.

2. Rheumatoid factor (RF) – autoantibodies to the Fc portion of IgG (mainly IgM); latex agglutination or nephelometry; occurs in rheumatoid arthritis but is not specific (other rheumatic diseases, infections, healthy elderly); anti-CCP is more specific.

slides.title: Determining CRP, RF, ASO. Clinical and diagnostic significance?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 3. ASO (antistreptolysin-O) – antibodies to streptolysin O of group A streptococcus; begin to rise ~1 week after infection, peak at 3–6 weeks; a sign of recent streptococcal infection (rheumatic fever, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis); dynamics in paired sera are important.
4. Disadvantages of latex tests: semi-quantitative, prozone effect, subjective reading; quantitative immunoturbidimetric methods are preferred in modern practice.
5. Results are interpreted with the clinical picture: RF/ASO alone is not a diagnosis.
